{{Short description|Main national census of Mexico}}
The '''Censo de Población y Vivienda''' (''Population and Housing Census'') is the main national population [[census]] for [[Mexico]]. It is compiled by the [[National Institute of Statistics and Geography]] (INEGI), a decentralized agency of the [[Government of Mexico|Mexican Federal government]], with the purpose of collating and reporting detailed [[demography|demographic]], [[socioeconomic]] and [[geography|geographical]] data from across the nation, and is conducted every ten years.

As of 2021, there have been a total of 14 national population censuses, [[2020 INEGI census|the most recent completed in 2020]].<ref name="inegi-census">{{cite web|url=https://www.inegi.org.mx/programas/ccpv/2020/default.html|title=Censos y Conteos de Población y Vivienda|language=es|publisher=INEGI|access-date=March 15, 2021}}</ref>

==History==
===Pre-Columbian era===
[[File:Xolotl_en_Tenayocan_L3.png|thumb|150px|left|Xolotl in Tenayuca.]]
The practice of census-taking in Mexico may have precedents dating back to the late [[pre-Columbian]] period. According to traditions recorded in several of the [[Spanish conquest of Mexico|post-conquest]] historical sources, [[King Xolotl|Xólotl]], a 12th-century ruler of a [[Chichimec]] polity in the [[Valley of Mexico]], ordered a review to be undertaken to enumerate the populace under his control. This survey was carried out close to its capital, [[Tenayuca]], at a locality subsequently named ''Nepōhualco'' in [[Classical Nahuatl]], meaning "place of enumeration".

The count was conducted by adding stones to a pile representing each person counted, giving a total of 3,200,000 residents.<ref name="inegi-history">{{cite web|url=https://www.inegi.org.mx/rnm/index.php/catalog/71|title=Red Nacional de Metadatos - Antecedentes|language=es|publisher=INEGI|access-date=March 15, 2021}}</ref> The retelling of this tradition was documented in the late 18th century by Francesco Clavigero, based on [[Fray Juan de Torquemada]]'s ''Monarchia Indiana'', first published in 1615.<ref name="clavigero">{{cite book |author=Clavigero, Francesco Saverio   |author-link=Francisco Javier Clavijero |year=1807 |orig-year=1787 |title=The history of Mexico. Collected from Spanish and Mexican historians, from manuscripts, and ancient paintings of the Indians. Illustrated by charts, and other copper plates. To which are added, critical dissertations on the land, the animals, and inhabitants of Mexico, 2 vols. |edition=2nd|others=Translated from the original Italian, by Charles Cullen, Esq. |location=London |publisher=[[Joseph Johnson (publisher)|J. Johnson]] |oclc=54014738}}</ref> Clavigero himself goes on to doubt some of what Torquemada wrote on the tale, citing aspects of it as "incredible". Nepohualco and the survey is also referenced in the codex [[Historia Tolteca-Chichimeca]], folio 33R.<ref name="Wimmer">{{cite web |author=Wimmer, Alexis|year=2006 |title=NEPOHUALCO|url=http://sites.estvideo.net/malinal/1.hist/N.html#NEPOHUALCO |work=Dictionnaire de la langue nahuatl classique |format=online version, incorporating reproductions from ''Dictionnaire de la langue nahuatl ou mexicaine'' [1885], by [[Rémi Siméon]]|access-date=2008-07-10}} {{in lang|fr|nah}}</ref>

During the later [[Aztec Empire]], it is known that written census-like records were used to keep track of land ownership and the [[tribute]] obligations of individual city-states (''[[altepetl]]'') across central Mexico.<ref name="smith">{{cite book |author=Smith, Michael E.|author-link=Michael E. Smith (archaeologist)|year=2003|title=The Aztecs|edition=2nd |publisher=[[Blackwell Publishing]]|location=Malden, MA |isbn=0-631-23015-7 |oclc=48579073}}</ref>

===Spanish rule===
In the decades after the conquest and Spanish colonial expansion, the administrators and missionaries for the [[Real Audiencia of Mexico|''Real Audiencia'' of Mexico]] began the systematic collection of population data for the new territories. One such was the document known as the ''Suma de visitas de pueblos por orden alfabético'' from 1548, which contained a survey and description of 907 villages and settlements in central Mexico.<ref name="carrera">{{cite journal |author=Carrera Stampa, Manuel|date=January 1968|title=Relaciones geográficas de Nueva España siglos XVI y XVIII |journal=Estudios de historia novohispana|url=http://www.ejournal.unam.mx/autor1.html?a=4119 |format=[[PDF]] online reproduction|volume=2 |pages=233–261|location=Mexico City|publisher=Instituto de Investigaciones Históricas – [[Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México]]|issn=0425-3574|oclc=1771954|language=es}}</ref>

A census taken twenty years later in 1568, covering about 90% of the towns and villages of Central Mexico, is probably the most comprehensive of the 16th-century recorded enumerations.<ref name="smith" /> During the later Colonial period in the 17th century a number of other demographic counts and compilations were made. In general the data from these, likely incomplete and rudimentary, are no longer preserved.<ref name="inegi-history" />

It was not until the late 18th century that an accounting of the population was conducted, known as the Revillagigedo census, the first poll to resemble a national census. Conducted under [[Viceroyalty of New Spain|viceroy]] [[Juan Vicente de Güemes Padilla Horcasitas y Aguayo, 2nd Count of Revillagigedo|Juan de Güemes Padilla, Count of Revillagigedo]] between 1790 and 1791, some forty volumes of data from this census are conserved in the Mexican national archives.<ref name="inegi-census" />

===Independence and modern era===
[[File:Constitucion 1824.PNG|thumb|150px|1824 Constitution.]]
After the [[Mexican War of Independence|Mexican independence]] from [[Spanish Empire|Spain]] was achieved in 1824, the new Republic sought a process to enumerate the citizens in each of its constituent [[federated states]] and entities.<ref name="vera">{{cite book|author=Vera Bolaños, Marta |author2=Rodrigo Pimienta Lastra|year=1998 |title=El registro de la población en el Estado de México durante el siglo XIX|url=http://polux.cmq.edu.mx/libreria/index.php?option=com_k2&view=item&id=107:el-registro-de-la-poblacion-en-el-estado-de-mexico&Itemid=229|format=[[PDF]] online reproduction |series=Documentos de Investigación, No. 12 |location=Zinacantepec, Mex. |publisher=[[:es:El Colegio Mexiquense|El Colegio Mexiquense]] |oclc=62300903 |language=es|access-date=March 15, 2021}}</ref>

Article 12 of the [[1824 Constitution of Mexico]] expressed this intention:
{{blockquote|
A census of the whole confederation shall be taken within five years, and shall be renewed afterward every ten years, which shall serve to designate the number of deputies to which each state is entitled. In the meantime, elections are to be regulated on the basis established in the preceding article, and the census which served to regulate the election of deputies in the Congress now in session.<ref name="const1824">{{cite web|url=https://tarlton.law.utexas.edu/constitutions/federal-mexican-1824-en|title=Federal Constitution of the United Mexican States (1824)|access-date=March 15, 2021}}</ref>
}}

The General Directorate of Statistics was created in 1882. The next year, it issued regulations establishing that the Directorate should conduct a general census of the country's inhabitants every ten years. In 1892, a pilot population census known as "Peñafiel Census" was carried out in Mexico City.<ref name="inegi-history" />

Under the presidency of Porfirio Díaz, the first national statistical enumeration was conducted in 1895, initiating the era of contemporary censuses.<ref name="inegi-history" />

Since 1900, the population census has been conducted on a [[decennial]] basis, taking place on the year ending in zero of each decade. The only variation to this schedule thus far occurred with the fourth census, where difficulties arising from the [[Mexican Revolution]] resulted in its deferral from 1920 to 1921.<ref name="inegi-census" />

In 1995 and 2005, INEGI compiled an intermediate series of national population and housing statistics, surveying only a selected subset of key [[demographic analysis|demographic indicators]]. Known as [[Conteo de Población y Vivienda|Nacional Population Count]] (''Conteo Nacional de Población''), they facilitated the planning for public policy and services by providing more up-to-date statistics than the decennial census. The 2015 count was replaced by an intercensal survey, although the INEGI does not consider that data as official population statistics.<ref name="inegi-census" />
